parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A small coil C has 64 turns and cross-sectional area $0.71\text{ cm}^2$. The coil is placed inside a solenoid as shown in Fig. 6.1.

{{figure:figure_6_1}}

Fig. 6.1

The centre of coil C is on the central axis of the solenoid.
parts.text:
There is a constant current in the solenoid.
Coil C is moved through the solenoid from position $X$ to position $Y$.

On Fig. 6.2, sketch a line to show the variation of the magnetic flux linkage in coil C with position as it moves from $X$ to $Y$.

{{figure:figure_6_2}}

Fig. 6.2

markscheme_points.text: non-zero horizontal straight line from X to Y

hints: Hint 1: Think about what the field is like on the central axis well inside a long solenoid carrying a steady current - does it get stronger or weaker as you move from X to Y?
parts.proper_answer: A horizontal straight line at a non-zero value of flux linkage from X to Y.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the field inside the solenoid**
You are moving the small coil along the central axis, staying well inside the solenoid. For a long solenoid with constant current, the magnetic flux density $B$ there is uniform - same strength and same direction everywhere along that central region.

Step 2: **Link to flux linkage**
Flux linkage for the small coil is $N\Phi = BAN$. Since $B$, $A$ and $N$ do not change as you slide from X to Y, the linkage stays constant. So on Fig. 6.2 you draw a flat, non-zero horizontal line.

hints: Hint 1: Start from the solenoid itself - with constant current, what can you say about $B$ at different points on its central axis between X and Y?
Hint 2: Now connect $B$ to what coil C links - which quantities in the linkage expression stay fixed while it moves?
parts.proper_answer: The magnetic flux density $B$ inside the solenoid is constant. Magnetic flux linkage $= BAN$ where $B$, $A$ and $N$ are all constant, so flux linkage is constant.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why B does not change**
A constant solenoid current produces a constant and uniform field inside. Between X and Y you are far from the ends, so the flux density $B$ that threads coil C is the same at every position.

Step 2: **Why linkage does not change**
For coil C, $$ \text{flux linkage} = BAN $$ $A = 0.71\text{ cm}^2$ and $N = 64$ are fixed properties of the coil, and $B$ is fixed by the argument above. A constant times constants is a constant, so the graph is flat.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text:
Coil C is now held stationary at $X$. The current in the solenoid varies so that the magnetic flux density $B$ at $X$ varies from time $0$ to time $4t$ as shown in Fig. 6.3.

{{figure:figure_6_3}}

Fig. 6.3

Calculate the maximum magnetic flux linkage in coil C.
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 6.3 and pick out the largest value of $B$ reached between time 0 and $4t$ - that is when linkage is largest.
Hint 2: Check the units of area before you multiply - how do you convert $0.71\text{ cm}^2$ into $\text{m}^2$ for use with $B$ in tesla?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify the maximum B**
From Fig. 6.3, $B$ rises from $0.040\text{ T}$ to a peak of $0.080\text{ T}$ at time $2t$, then falls. So $B_{max} = 0.080\text{ T}$. Maximum linkage occurs there.

Step 2: **Apply NPhi = BAN with SI units**
Convert area: $$ A = 0.71\text{ cm}^2 = 0.71 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2 $$ Then: $$ \text{flux linkage}_{max} = B_{max}AN = 0.080 \times 0.71 \times 10^{-4} \times 64 $$ $$ = 3.6 \times 10^{-4}\text{ Wb} $$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (a)(iv)

markscheme_points.text: sketch showing: $E$ is zero from time 0 to time $t$ and non-zero after time $t$
$E$ has constant non-zero magnitude between time $t$ and time $4t$
$E$ has non-zero value of one sign between time $t$ and time $2t$, and non-zero value of the opposite sign between time $2t$ and time $4t$

hints: Hint 1: Recall that induced e.m.f. depends on rate of change of linkage, not the linkage itself - in which time interval in Fig. 6.3 is $B$ not changing at all?
Hint 2: Compare the steepness of the $B$-t graph from $t$ to $2t$ with that from $2t$ to $4t$ - what does equal steepness but opposite slope tell you about size and sign of $E$?
Hint 3: Think about what happens to the sign of the gradient when $B$ stops rising and starts falling - how must $E$ change at time $2t$?
parts.proper_answer: $E = 0$ from $0$ to $t$. $E$ is constant non-zero from $t$ to $2t$ and constant non-zero of opposite sign from $2t$ to $4t$, with equal magnitude from $t$ to $4t$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Faraday's law as a gradient rule**
You know $$ E = -\frac{\Delta(N\Phi)}{\Delta t} = -NA\frac{\Delta B}{\Delta t} $$ So $E$ is proportional to minus the gradient of the $B$-time graph. Flat $B$ means zero $E$. Steep $B$ means large $E$.

Step 2: **Zero e.m.f. first**
From $0$ to $t$, $B = 0.040\text{ T}$ constant. Gradient is zero, so rate of change of linkage is zero and $$ E = 0 $$

Step 3: **Equal and opposite constant e.m.f. after**
From $t$ to $2t$, $B$ rises linearly $0.040 \to 0.080\text{ T}$ in time $t$. Gradient is positive constant, so $E$ is constant of one sign. From $2t$ to $4t$, $B$ falls linearly $0.080 \to 0$ in time $2t$. The drop of $0.080\text{ T}$ in $2t$ is a gradient of $-0.040/t$, equal in magnitude to the rise of $+0.040/t$. So $E$ is constant with the same magnitude but opposite sign. At $2t$ the line jumps across the time axis.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A metal spring rests on a smooth table. The turns of the spring are equally spaced. The ends of the spring are connected to a d.c. power supply, as shown in Fig. 6.5.

{{figure:figure_6_5}}

Fig. 6.5

The spring is connected to the d.c. power supply using flexible leads. The spring is not under tension.

With reference to magnetic fields, describe and explain the change in the distance between the turns of the spring when the power supply is first switched on.

markscheme_points.text: current in spring creates a magnetic field around the spring

either (magnetic) fields around adjacent turns interact to cause a force to be exerted (between the turns) or current in one turn interacts with (magnetic) field due to adjacent turns to cause force to be exerted (between the turns)
(magnetic force) is attractive so distance (between turns) decreases

hints: Hint 1: Start with a single turn - what surrounds any wire when a d.c. current is switched on in it?
Hint 2: Now place two turns side by side - how can the current in one turn feel a force due to what the neighbouring turn produces?
Hint 3: Think of two parallel wires carrying current in the same direction - do they attract or repel, and what does that do to the spacing of the spring?
parts.proper_answer: Current in the spring produces magnetic fields around the turns. The current in one turn interacts with the field from an adjacent turn, exerting a magnetic force between turns. Currents are in the same sense so the force is attractive and the separation between turns decreases - the spring compresses.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Current makes a field**
As soon as the supply is on, each turn of the metal spring is a current-carrying loop. Every current creates its own magnetic field around it.

Step 2: **Neighbouring turns exert forces on each other**
Think of adjacent turns as parallel wires. The magnetic field due to one turn acts on the current in the next turn, giving a motor-type force $F = BIL$ between them. This is the interaction of fields and currents of neighbouring coils.

Step 3: **Direction is attractive**
On the same side of the spring, current in adjacent turns flows in the same direction. Parallel co-directional currents attract magnetically. So each turn is pulled toward its neighbours, the distance between turns decreases and the spring shortens on its smooth table.
